title: Two MAC addresses for one gateway

alerts.title: IDS: gateway 192.0.2.1 answered ARP from two MAC addresses on the finance VLAN; unsolicited replies from 02:42:ac:11:00:66
Help desk: five finance users report certificate warnings on the intranet; two clicked through
Timesheet app: payroll administrator session reused from 192.0.2.66
IDS: plain-text logins to the timesheet app captured on the finance VLAN by 192.0.2.66

MAC table: 02:42:ac:11:00:66 on port Gi1/0/14 (conference room 3 wall jack); 192.0.2.66 by DHCP
Span capture running: gratuitous ARP replies every 2 seconds from Gi1/0/14
Small computer behind the conference-room printer, photographed, bagged and logged by the security officer

secondaryObjectives: Analyze application-level and network-level session hijacking and choose countermeasures

brief.situation: You are a network security analyst at Corbel Engineering, a fictional firm. At 10:00 the IDS reports the finance VLAN's gateway address answering from two MAC addresses, and finance staff say the intranet keeps showing certificate warnings. The timesheet app on that VLAN still uses plain HTTP. Find the cause, stop it, keep the evidence, close what it exposed, and write it up.
handover: You can change switch configuration, end application sessions and force password resets under the network security procedure. Physical evidence goes to the security officer.
This is your own network: everything here is defensive work on systems you are responsible for.
howItWorks: Each task takes time: choose it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you close the incident you notify, record it and explain your reasoning.

source.note: Fifteen minutes until a captured session cookie is reused is the author's figure.
Twenty minutes until plain-text passwords are captured is the author's figure.
Thirty-five minutes until the hijacked session exports the pay table is the author's figure.

effects.finding: The gateway's address resolves to 02:42:ac:11:00:66 on finance PCs, not to the router: ARP cache poisoning. Traffic, including the timesheet app's plain-HTTP cookies, passes through that device.

trace.label: Trace the unknown MAC to its switch port

effects.log: You look the MAC up in the switch's address table.

capture.label: Start a packet capture on the finance VLAN's span port

effects.log: The span port captures the VLAN's traffic, including the forged ARP replies, with times.

shutPort.label: Shut down switch port Gi1/0/14
shutPort.available: not busy and isNull(portAt) and (not isNull(traceAt))

effects.log: The port is down. The device is cut off and the finance PCs relearn the real gateway.

clearArp.label: Clear the ARP caches on the finance PCs
clearArp.why: Finish the task in progress first.

effects.log: {poisoning ? "Caches cleared. Within seconds the forged replies poison them again: the device is still sending." : "Caches cleared; the real gateway is learned."}

dai.label: Enable DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection on the finance VLAN

effects.log: Switches now drop ARP replies that do not match the DHCP binding table. Forged gateway replies stop working from any port.

seize.label: Have the security officer photograph, bag and log the device
seize.available: not busy and isNull(deviceAt) and (not isNull(traceAt) and isNull(wipeAt))

wipe.label: Have IT unplug the device and reimage it for reuse
wipe.available: not busy and isNull(wipeAt) and (not isNull(traceAt) and isNull(deviceAt))

effects.log: IT unplugs the device and reimages it. Poisoning stops, and with it every trace of who set it up and what it collected.

resetCreds.why: Finish the task in progress first.

writeup.question: For the incident record: what the attack was and how you knew, how you stopped it, and what it exposed.

parts.label: Recognition and detection
parts.criteria: Names ARP cache poisoning from the evidence (one IP, two MACs; unsolicited replies; certificate warnings as interception), not MAC flooding or DHCP starvation, and traces the MAC to a port.
parts.modelAnswer: The gateway's IP resolved to an unknown MAC with unsolicited replies, and users saw certificate warnings: ARP poisoning for an adversary in the middle, traced to Gi1/0/14.

parts.label: Countermeasure
parts.criteria: Stops it at the port (clearing caches alone is undone in seconds), keeps a capture and the device in custody instead of wiping it, and enables DHCP snooping with Dynamic ARP Inspection so it cannot recur from another port.
parts.modelAnswer: I captured first, shut the port, had the device bagged with a custody log, and enabled DHCP snooping and DAI on the VLAN.

parts.label: Hijacking
parts.criteria: Ends the app's sessions and resets passwords exposed in plain text; fixes the cause with HTTPS and Secure, HttpOnly cookies.
parts.modelAnswer: I ended every timesheet session and reset the exposed passwords; the app moves to HTTPS with Secure and HttpOnly cookies so a sniffed cookie is useless.

expertPath.text: Read the ARP tables: the gateway's IP on an unknown MAC. Start a capture. Trace the MAC to Gi1/0/14.
Shut the port; end the timesheet sessions as a precaution.
Enable DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection; have the device bagged with a custody log.
Move the app to HTTPS with Secure, HttpOnly cookies; tell finance the warnings were real; record it.

handled.headline: Good: recognized, cut, kept, hardened
handled.body: One IP on two MACs with certificate warnings is ARP poisoning. The port stopped it, the capture and device kept it, and DAI keeps it from coming back.

handledCostly.headline: Stopped, with gaps
handledCostly.body: The criteria show what cost you: a session or passwords taken first, missing evidence, or a VLAN still open to the same trick.

dataTaken.headline: The session was used
dataTaken.body: Clearing caches is undone in seconds while the device sends. Cut it at the port, and end sessions that crossed in the clear.

evidenceLost.headline: Evidence reimaged
evidenceLost.body: A rogue device is evidence: photograph, bag and log it. Wiping it erased who placed it and what it took.

leftOpen.headline: Something still works for the attacker
leftOpen.body: Poisoning, a hijacked session or captured passwords: close all three before you close the case.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No incident record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: One gateway IP answering from two MACs, unsolicited ARP replies and certificate warnings point to ARP cache poisoning for an adversary in the middle. Start a capture, trace the MAC to its port and shut it (clearing caches is undone in seconds). End the app's sessions and reset any passwords that crossed in plain text. Keep the device as evidence with a custody log rather than wiping it. Enable DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection so a forged reply is dropped from any port, and move the app to HTTPS with Secure, HttpOnly cookies.
